1: This briefing is Book 12 of the Federal Modernization Workbook, Security Operations and Telemetry.
It's about how an agency makes every part of its estate emit evidence, turns that evidence into detection and response, and then proves it all works.
Why can't you defend what you can't see?
What must each plane emit, and how do findings reach one queue?
And how do you run detection, response and monitoring?
The short version: design visibility instead of assuming it, and close a finding only when the thing is actually fixed, with proof.
The slides and notes carry every detail and source; I'll stick to what matters.
Let's start with why visibility can't be assumed.
2: Most agencies run a sim, pay for log storage, and can show an auditor millions of events a day.
But every one of those numbers measures what arrived.
None of them measures what didn't.
nist keeps apart two things that are easy to buy as one.
One control says generate the audit records.
Others say review them, analyze them and detect attacks.
An agency can satisfy the first completely and still fail the rest.
O M B's logging memo, M-26-14, measures the same way.
It sets retention floors, but its maturity model scores collection by alerting, by how much of the baseline is covered by actionable alerts.
And here's the sharp example: Microsoft says logs sent only to the Sentinel data lake tier don't generate alerts.
That source meets retention and detects nothing.
3: Coverage gaps don't announce themselves, and there are four ways they stay quiet.
Some sources are never connected; Azure resource logs aren't collected until each resource gets a diagnostic setting.
Some connected sources aren't flowing; a green connector status can mean a rule exists, not that data arrived.
Some collected data is never analyzed.
And some sources are switched off on purpose, which sis-uh calls well-documented attacker behavior.
In the 2023 Exchange Online intrusion, a federal victim caught it with its own alert on mailbox events that, at the time, came only with a premium license.
Agencies without those events had nothing to look at.
None of these gaps shows up in what arrived, only in comparing it with what was expected.
That's why the inventory is the denominator.
4: A multi-cloud agency runs several stacks at once: Azure, AWS, a virtualization manager, firewall syslog, a Linux agent.
Five partial views can't prove that one vulnerability is fixed everywhere.
The program's answer is an evidence contract: one record shape that every source emits, with eight fields fixed before any data flows.
They carry what nist asks an audit record to establish, plus the control it evidences, a verdict and a disposition.
The join key is authoritative asset identity plus time.
Every stack has its own identifier, so the key comes from the naming plane, which has to exist before the pipeline.
And time means when the state was observed, because joining on arrival time silently matches the wrong records.
One caution: the system-wide, time-correlated trail is a High-baseline control, so at Moderate the program selects it by design.
Next, what each plane must emit.
5: The program treats the estate as six planes: identity, cloud platform, Microsoft 365, endpoints, network and data.
No single plane covers the logging baseline, and systems a third party runs for the agency are in scope too.
Each plane has a default that looks instrumented and isn't.
Entra ID shows sign-ins, but keeps them only 30 days, so the program streams every sign-in stream, not just the interactive one.
Azure drops its activity log after 90 days, and resource logs aren't collected at all without a diagnostic setting.
Microsoft 365 audit retention depends on license, and many users, guests included, get the shorter window.
So emission is enforced by policy, and verified by a query that names every expected table.
That way, a missing table shows up as a row, instead of silently disappearing.
Next, turning the warehouse into detection.
6: A workspace full of tables is still a warehouse.
Rules, incidents and automation are what turn it into a detection engine.
And the program's rule is strict: no source counts as monitored until an enabled rule reads it, and no rule counts until its output reaches a queue someone owns.
The engine also sets a floor on how fast you can detect.
Scheduled rules run every few minutes at best, near-real-time rules are faster but limited in number, and behavioral baselines are slower by design; the slide has the figures.
Defender XDR detects what its own sensors see on endpoints, identities and email.
Sentinel rules cover what Defender can't see, like D N S and other clouds.
Then prepare for the assessor's test: show a recent alert, the incident it opened, and what was done, from alert to closure.
7: Two federal clocks run against this work.
The first is sis-uh's BOD 26-04, issued in June 2026.

It replaced the older vulnerability directives, and swapped severity buckets for four questions about each vulnerable asset: is it publicly exposed, is the flaw known to be exploited, can exploitation be automated, and how much control does it give?
The answers set a maximum timeline, as short as three days, with forensic triage on the worst cases, because applying a patch doesn't evict an attacker.
The clock starts when sis-uh lists the flaw or the agency finds it, whichever comes first, and there are no waivers.
Remediation within the table applies from December 7.
The second clock is M-26-14's: a logging plan within 90 days of sis-uh's reference architecture, then maturity levels on a set schedule.
8: Vulnerability management fails at three points assessors probe: a stale inventory, prioritizing by score alone, and no record of when something was found, due and fixed.
The program's answer is a daily queue.

Pull the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities feed and the scanner's findings, join each device to the authoritative asset record and its exposure tag, apply the directive's table, and keep the first-detected date, never resetting it.
Two practical rules: treat an asset with no exposure tag as publicly exposed, and keep your own history, because the scanner's exports don't.
The key idea is that a scanner authors no state; it just measures a gap.
Each platform patches with its own native tools, but every one returns the same remediation record, keyed to the same asset.
A finding closes when the fix is recorded and the next scan no longer sees it.
9: Three more streams share the same queue.
Configuration first: a patched host that drifts from its baseline isn't remediated.
And watch auto-correct features that fix drift without recording it; the program keeps those for low-risk settings.
A storage account open to the internet has no missing patch, so a vulnerability scanner never reports it.
Each provider's native posture tool is primary for its own platform, and the notes cover where cross-cloud coverage falls short.
Controlled unclassified information comes in two levels, Basic and Specified, decided by the CUI Registry, and labels drive data loss prevention everywhere.
Finally, check what actually reaches the queue.
Since October 2026, a built-in Microsoft tuning rule keeps data loss signals out of the incident queue unless an administrator turns it off.
10: Most agencies can name their SOC. Fewer can say who decided that a log source is collected, how long it's kept, or who accepted the risk when it went quiet for three weeks.
The C I O sets scope and funding.
The see-so decides what each plane must emit, owns the logging plan, and approves any playbook that acts on production.
Platform owners keep their planes emitting, security engineering builds the tooling, and the SOC runs the queue.
Two roles are easy to forget.
The records officer must agree before anyone shortens retention, because evidence that's gone can't come back.
And the authorizing official, the only one who can accept risk, accepts the risk of not seeing: a gap carried rather than closed, a suppression with no end date, a missed deadline.
11: The rule library lives in version control, nobody edits a production rule in the portal, and every change is a reviewed commit.
Each rule has one named owner, a test and a review date.
Every rule moves through five steps: author it, test it, run it alert-only, promote it, and review it at least quarterly.
Replay a known-bad sample, because a rule that can't be shown to fire isn't finished.
And run it alert-only for at least two weeks, until its false positives are documented.
Where a vendor analytic isn't available in the agency's cloud, the program builds an equivalent inside its own boundary, and says plainly it isn't parity.
Thresholds drift, sources stop without an error, and failing rules get disabled.
That standing tuning effort is the real cost of a library.
12: Detection without response shortens the investigation, not the exposure.
So every playbook is gated by confidence: high confidence prepares containment, medium confidence enriches and opens a ticket for a human, and low confidence never acts.
Responses sit on the workbook's actuation ladder, from observing and advising, up to gated actuation, where the playbook prepares an action and a named approver releases it.
That's the default for anything with a large blast radius.
Only listed, low-risk classes run on their own, logged and reversible.
A few, like isolating a server or disabling a privileged account, always need an approver.
And because Defender's attack disruption acts on its own, the authorizing official decides whether to accept that.
A hybrid user must be disabled in Active Directory as well, or the next sync undoes it.
13: Continuous monitoring is a pipeline: emit, normalize, correlate, bind each record to its control, report, and respond.
The metrics are built so they can't flatter.
Detection coverage counts how many baseline activities have an enabled, tested rule over a fresh source, not how many rules exist.
A stale required source counts as a failure.
Vulnerability metrics count closures on time plus items past due, because a percentage of the open queue improves every time new findings arrive.
And configuration reports passing, failing and excepted settings separately.
The logging memo scores a system at its weakest element, and fed-ramp's Key Security Indicators bind cloud providers, not agencies.
In the end, a finding closes on re-test evidence, or the authorizing official carries it with an end date.
14: Name the planes and assets that are expected to emit, and check each one against what actually arrives.
Stand up the naming plane before the evidence pipeline, so every record joins on one asset identity.
Fund the logging plan as the program's visibility plan, not as a storage purchase.
And send every blind spot to the authorizing official, whether it's a telemetry gap, an open-ended suppression or a missed deadline, each with an end date.
The next step needs no procurement.
Run the coverage check against the inventory, tag the exposure of every externally reachable asset before December 7, and count a source as covered only when a tested rule reads it.
You can't defend what you can't see, and a finding closes only when the thing is fixed, with proof.
